newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: MORE RAIN WORRIES MAY LIFT S.AFRICA MAIZE PRICES.
newsitem.headline: MORE RAIN WORRIES MAY LIFT S.AFRICA MAIZE PRICES.

text.p: Forecasts of more rain in the northeast and eastern parts of South Africa may prop up spot maize prices this week as the harvest -- already delayed by over a month -- is stalled again, industry analysts said on Monday.

Following unseasonal rains into June, maize from the 1997 crop had started to trickle in after recent drier weather, but the start of a sudden cold snap on Sunday and the threat of showers in the maize-growing belt may derail harvest efforts.

"If there is more rain, then I can see prices of both white and yellow maize coming up," said Rod Blondin, general manager of the agricultural markets division of the South African Futures Exchange (Safex).

The Weather Services Corp said in its daily report on Monday that light to moderate showers were expected in the northeast of the country, spreading to the east on Tuesday and south on Friday. Temperatures were seen trending cooler.
July yellow maize on Safex added three rand early on Monday to trade at 555 rand from 552 settlement on Friday. July white was bid at 575 rand and offered at 600 from 575 settlement.

Giel van Zyl of the National Maize Producers Organisation said last week that harvesting in the eastern parts of the country was especially slow as fields were still too wet. In other parts the moisture content of plants was too high.

Despite the harvest delay, maize spot and near-month prices have been drifting lower over the past few months on expectations of a one to two million tonne domestic surplus and forecasts of the second biggest ever U.S. corn crop.

But analysts said that, in addition to the possible price-inflating impact of continued rains, recent downside was seen capped by the possibility of rain damage and export commitments, especially on white maize.
Views on crop damage were mixed with some analysts saying that yields had been unaffected and that quality was only slightly below last year's healthy crop. But others disagreed.

"There are quality problems with most of the white maize that has been harvested, so there may be less WM1 from white. This could maybe cause a glut of yellow as poor damaged white flows over to the animal feed market," one trader said.
A co-operative based in the east of the country said that yellow maize was producing some poor quality WM3's, which were not seen last year.
South Africa's official monthly maize crop estimate was last week left unchanged at 7.660 million tonnes due to a lack of new data as a result of the harvest delay, the forecast body said.
Export commitments of especially white maize, which traders said was attracting higher offshore prices than yellow was seen supporting white prices, whilst weighing further on yellow.
At least 70,000 tonnes of white maize had already been sent to drought-hit Kenya with more designated for shipment later.

Traders said there were rumours that export contracts on small batches of yellow had also been concluded, with destinations likely to be the traditional markets of Iran, the United Arab Emirates and Mauritius.
Grain co-ops said this month that more than 70 percent of this year's surplus, which is estimated at between one and two million tonnes, has already been sold to the export market.

Trade in maize this week was seen quiet amid the slow harvest -- barring a major weather scare. Graham Voller, Safex's operations manager told Reuters that open interest on all Safex maize contracts, covering the months from July 1997 to March 1998 last week rose by only 100 contracts to a total 2,716.
Monday also sees the start of physical delivery on the July contract of Safex, which although primarily a hedging market allows this option.
South Africa's 1997 commercial crop is well below last year's bumper output of 9.694 million tonnes.
-- Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
